after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find the range of the function $f(x)=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})-1.$
after.worked_solution:
The range of $\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ consists of two intervals:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})\le -1,\,\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})\ge 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

- Multiplying the first interval by $\frac{1}{3}$ and subtracting $1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})\le -1 \\  & \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})\le -\frac{1}{3} \\  & \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})-1\le -\frac{1}{3}-1 \\  & f(x)\le -\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Multiplying the second interval by $\frac{1}{3}$ and subtracting $1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})\ge 1 \\  & \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})\ge \frac{1}{3} \\  & \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})-1\ge \frac{1}{3}-1 \\  & f(x)\ge -\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get

$$
f(x)\le -\frac{4}{3},\,f(x)\ge -\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the range is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,-\frac{4}{3}]\cup [-\frac{2}{3},\infty ).$

content.problem: Find the range of the function $f(x)=\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})-1.$
content.worked_solution:
The range of $\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ consists of two intervals:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})\le -1,\,\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})\ge 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

- Multiplying the first interval by $\frac{1}{3}$ and subtracting $1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})\le -1 \\  & \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})\le -\frac{1}{3} \\  & \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})-1\le -\frac{1}{3}-1 \\  & f(x)\le -\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Multiplying the second interval by $\frac{1}{3}$ and subtracting $1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})\ge 1 \\  & \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})\ge \frac{1}{3} \\  & \frac{1}{3}\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{\pi }{8})-1\ge \frac{1}{3}-1 \\  & f(x)\ge -\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get

$$
f(x)\le -\frac{4}{3},\,f(x)\ge -\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the range is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,-\frac{4}{3}]\cup [-\frac{2}{3},\infty ).$

after.problem: Find the range of the function $f(x)=5\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})-3.$
after.worked_solution:
The range of $\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ consists of two intervals:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\le -1,\,\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\ge 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

- Multiplying the first interval by $5$ and subtracting $3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\le -1 \\  & 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\le -5 \\  & 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})-3\le -5-3 \\  & f(x)\le -8.\end{aligned}
$$

- Multiplying the second interval by $5$ and subtracting $3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\ge 1 \\  & 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\ge 5 \\  & 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})-3\ge 5-3 \\  & f(x)\ge 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get

$$
f(x)\le -8,\,f(x)\ge 2.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the range is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,-8]\cup [2,\infty ).$

content.problem: Find the range of the function $f(x)=5\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})-3.$
content.worked_solution:
The range of $\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ consists of two intervals:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\le -1,\,\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\ge 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

- Multiplying the first interval by $5$ and subtracting $3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\le -1 \\  & 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\le -5 \\  & 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})-3\le -5-3 \\  & f(x)\le -8.\end{aligned}
$$

- Multiplying the second interval by $5$ and subtracting $3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\ge 1 \\  & 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\ge 5 \\  & 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})-3\ge 5-3 \\  & f(x)\ge 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get

$$
f(x)\le -8,\,f(x)\ge 2.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the range is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,-8]\cup [2,\infty ).$

after.problem: What is the domain of the function $f(x)=-\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})?$ Assume that $n$ is an integer.
after.worked_solution:
The domain of $y=\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ consists of all values where $\operatorname{sin}⁡x\ne 0,$ and is given by the expression

$$
x\ne n\pi ,
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

To find the domain of $-\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}),$ we replace the $x$ on the left-hand side of the above with $(\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}).$ This gives

$$
\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}\ne n\pi .
$$

Solving for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{6} & \ne n\pi  \\ \frac{2x}{3} & \ne \frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi  \\ 2x & \ne \frac{3\pi }{6}+3n\pi  \\ 2x & \ne \frac{\pi }{2}+3n\pi  \\ x & \ne \frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{3n\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain of the function is $x\ne \frac{\pi }{4}+3n\frac{\pi }{2},$ where $n$ is an integer.

content.problem: What is the domain of the function $f(x)=-\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{6})?$ Assume that $n$ is an integer.
content.worked_solution:
The domain of $y=\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ consists of all values where $\operatorname{sin}⁡x\ne 0,$ and is given by the expression

$$
x\ne n\pi ,
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

To find the domain of $-\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}),$ we replace the $x$ on the left-hand side of the above with $(\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}).$ This gives

$$
\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{6}\ne n\pi .
$$

Solving for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{\pi }{6} & \ne n\pi  \\ \frac{2x}{3} & \ne \frac{\pi }{6}+n\pi  \\ 2x & \ne \frac{3\pi }{6}+3n\pi  \\ 2x & \ne \frac{\pi }{2}+3n\pi  \\ x & \ne \frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{3n\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain of the function is $x\ne \frac{\pi }{4}+3n\frac{\pi }{2},$ where $n$ is an integer.
